# What is machine learning?

## A machine is a recipe

A *machine*, for our purposes, is anything that turns an **input** into an **output** by following a fixed recipe. A thermostat turns a temperature into "heat on" or "heat off". A spreadsheet formula turns a column of numbers into their average. Your microwave turns "2 minutes, high" into a hot burrito. None of these machines *learn*: give them the same input tomorrow and they will do exactly the same thing.

## Learning is changing the recipe

*Learning* means the recipe improves with experience. Show a learning machine a few hundred examples of inputs paired with the outputs you wanted, and it adjusts its internal parameters (the *weights*, or knobs) until its outputs match yours more closely. The real test is whether that tuned recipe generalizes to inputs it has **never seen**.

Memorizing examples can be part of a learning algorithm, as in nearest-neighbor methods. The practical question is whether the resulting predictions work on new observations. A fixed formula whose behavior never changes with experience does not learn from data.

::: {.callout-tip .takeaway title="Takeaway #1"}
Learning uses experience to shape a model; held-out evaluation tests whether that model generalizes.
:::

## Learning is rolling downhill

How does a machine know which way to turn its knobs? It evaluates an **error** (or **loss**): a single number measuring how far the machine's current predictions fall from the target outputs. Plotting error across every possible knob setting forms a landscape of hills and valleys. Gradient-based training takes steps intended to reduce the objective; it can converge to a local solution or fail to converge.

The standard descent algorithm, **gradient descent**, uses only local information: measure the slope of the error surface at the current position, take a step in the steepest downhill direction, and repeat. The size of that step is the **learning rate**. Press play below, try a larger step size, and drag the ball to different starting points.

```{python}
#| label: w-error-landscape
#| echo: false
show("error_landscape")
```

With a tiny step size, the ball settles into the first valley it encounters and stays there, even when a deeper basin sits just across the ridge. That shallow valley is a **local minimum**; the lowest point on the entire surface is the **global minimum**. Larger steps can carry the ball across small ridges, while steps that are too large overshoot the valley walls and oscillate without converging.

::: {.callout-tip .takeaway title="Takeaway #2"}
Many learning methods optimize an objective, but a global optimum is not guaranteed and need not give the best generalization.
:::

Optimization provides a useful framework for several methods here: regression fits coefficients, K-means updates centroids, and autoencoders minimize reconstruction loss. Other methods use different procedures: nearest-neighbor classification stores examples, and hierarchical clustering repeatedly merges clusters. Their objectives and guarantees must be considered separately.

# Regression: Predict a Number

Regression predicts a continuous quantity from one or more measurements: a household's total expenditure from health and demographic indicators, a child's reading score from perinatal risk factors, or productive vocabulary size from age in months. In linear regression, the knobs set the slope and intercept of a straight line (or a flat hyperplane across many predictors), and the error is the sum of squared vertical distances between the line and the observed points.

## Fit a Line by Eye

Drag the two round handles (or grab the line itself) until the fit looks right. Each orange square shows a **residual** — the vertical miss for one observation — drawn as a literal square proportional to the residual in screen coordinates. The meter in the corner sums the areas of all those squares.

```{python}
#| label: w-ols-fit
#| echo: false
show("ols_fit")
```

Click **show best line** to compare your eye fit against the analytic optimum, or **snap to least squares** to animate your line to the minimum-error solution. Because **ordinary least squares** (OLS) minimizes the sum of *squared* residuals, a residual twice as large contributes four times as much area, making large residuals costly. Leverage specifically concerns extreme predictor values, which can make observations influential when combined with their residuals.

## Fit a Line by Rolling Downhill

A straight line has a closed-form algebraic solution, but most machine learning models do not. To bridge the two worlds, we can fit the exact same line by gradient descent. Because a line has two knobs (slope and intercept), the error landscape is a two-dimensional bowl: darker contours mark lower error, and the gold star marks the least-squares minimum.

```{python}
#| label: w-gd-regression
#| echo: false
show("gd_regression")
```

Click anywhere on the contour map to initialize a new starting line, then press play. A moderate learning rate tracks smoothly down the valley floor to the star; an overly large learning rate zig-zags across the canyon walls or diverges.

::: {.callout-tip .takeaway title="Takeaway #3"}
A model is a parameterized family of functions. Training adjusts the parameters to minimize error.
:::

## Non-linear Regression: Bending the Line with Splines

Relationships in biological and developmental data are often nonlinear. Average vocabulary production changes with age, while children differ substantially at each age. The position and shape of any apparent acceleration depend on the population and measurement instrument. Dose-response curves may saturate, and acoustic signals can oscillate.

One way to model curvature is a global polynomial, which we examine in the cross-validation section. High-degree polynomials can become unstable near boundaries or outside the observed range; this depends on the data, degree, and regularization.

A **spline** solves this by working *locally*. Divide the input axis at a set of landmark points called **knots**, and fit simple low-degree pieces between them:

- A **piecewise-linear spline** (degree 1) connects the knots with straight line segments, like a carpenter's folding ruler.
- A **cubic spline** (degree 3) joins smooth cubic curves at the knots so that both the slope and curvature match continuously across every joint.

```{python}
#| label: w-spline-scaling
#| echo: false
show("spline_scaling")
```

Press play (or scrub the segment count $K$) in Figure 4 above. The left panel shows a smooth multi-frequency target curve tiled by $K$ piecewise segments; the right panel plots the mean squared error (MSE) against $K$ on log-log axes. Each time you double the number of segments, the width of each piece halves ($h \propto K^{-1}$), and for a piecewise-linear fit on a smooth curve the approximation error can approach the asymptotic rate $\text{MSE} \propto K^{-4}$. Switch the data toggle in the widget gallery (or pass real data below) to see the same resolution scaling on child vocabulary growth, where training reconstruction error and between-child variability should be distinguished. Increasing flexibility alone does not demonstrate better held-out prediction.

### From Splines to Neural Networks: A Bank of ReLU Hinges

How do you write a piecewise-linear spline so a linear regression solver can fit it? Instead of fitting separate equations on each interval, you build a **basis** of **hinge functions** — one at each knot $\kappa_j$:

$$h_j(x) = \max(0,\, x - \kappa_j)$$

Each hinge stays flat at zero to the left of its knot $\kappa_j$ and rises with unit slope to the right. Adding a weighted sum of hinges to a baseline line bends the slope at every knot:

$$\hat{y}(x) = w_0 + w_1 x + \sum_{j=1}^{K} v_j \max(0,\, x - \kappa_j)$$

If you have ever heard of a **Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU)** in deep learning, you are looking right at it: $\text{ReLU}(z) = \max(0, z)$ is a hinge function. The difference between classical spline regression and a single-layer ReLU neural network comes down to *how the knots are chosen*:

- **Spline regression** places the knots $\kappa_j$ at fixed positions (equally spaced or at quantiles of $x$) and solves for the output weights $v_j$ in one step by least squares.
- **A neural network** treats the knot positions $\kappa_j$ as learnable weights too, using gradient descent to slide the hinges into the sharpest bends of the data — and then stacks multiple layers of hinges so the kinks can fold high-dimensional spaces.

Try both below: drag the orange knot pins along the horizontal axis by hand, or press **optimize knots (GD)** to watch gradient descent migrate the hinges toward the steepest bends.

```{python}
#| label: w-spline-relu-basis
#| echo: false
show("spline_relu_basis")
```

::: {.callout-tip .takeaway title="Takeaway #4"}
Spline regression combines basis functions to model curvature. A one-dimensional ReLU network represents a continuous piecewise-linear function whose breakpoints can be learned.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Measurement and interpretation"}
The perinatal stress index is a teaching composite constructed from neonatal health, gestation, birthweight, smoking, prenatal care, and maternal education, with manually chosen weights and full-sample scaling. It is not a validated maternal-stress measure. The externalizing score is not a specific attention scale. These observational examples do not identify causal effects. Predictive models below use the original covariates rather than the full-sample composite.
:::
